query: What are the exact inverse-Laplace/discrete-time mappings (closed-form) for DPLR SSMs including ZOH and Tustin variants, and what guidance maps sampling rate and discretization choice to time-kernel error?

response.query: What are the exact inverse-Laplace/discrete-time mappings (closed-form) for DPLR SSMs including ZOH and Tustin variants, and what guidance maps sampling rate and discretization choice to time-kernel error?
response.answer: The inverse-Laplace mappings for DPLR SSMs include ZOH and Tustin methods; ZOH uses (1 - z^-1) for discretization, while Tustin approximates using bilinear transform. Sampling rate choice impacts time-kernel error, with higher rates reducing error.

results.title: Efficient and interpretable raw audio classification with diagonal state space models | Machine Learning
results.content: In The International Conference on Learning Representations.")) recently proposed deep structured State Space Models (SSMs) motivated by Linear Time Invariant (LTI) continuous-time SSMs. The S4 model, along with its variants (DSS, S4D, S5, etc.) (Gu et al., 2024. In Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML’23.")) resurrects RNNs for long sequence tasks by proposing the Linear Recurrent Unit (LRU), which allows for the transfer of the inner working mechanics of deep SSMs towards discrete RNNs. Inference-wise, deep continuous-time SSMs overcome the \(O(T^2)\) bottleneck of attention layers by materializing the discrete variant of the LTI systems’ differential equations, which is equivalent to an RNN at inference time (Gu et al., 2022. Well-defined discretization rules, motivated by modern control systems, theoretically allow for switching dynamic behavior of the discrete system and enable inference on input data with different sampling rates without the need for retraining (Smith et al., 2023. * *Layer-wise Downsampling* Continuous-time SSMs allow for switching their discrete dynamics with the sampling rate during discretization. *Random Zero Order Hold Regularization* Modifying the internal sampling rate with layer-wise downsampling can lead to aliasing and discretization errors, which the network has not seen during training. *Interpretability of Complex-Valued SSMs* The parameters of diagonal SSM layers are commonly defined in the continuous-time domain with complex values (Orvieto et al., 2023. To improve training and inference speed, several authors proposed diagonal approximations of the state transition matrix initializations, resulting in S4D (Gu et al., 2024. These SSM layers are modeled as complex-valued continuous-time LTI systems (Smith et al., 2023. During training and inference, it is necessary to map the continuous system to a discrete version (e.g., via ZOH) with a learnable time-scale parameter \(\Delta ~\!\!\in ~\!\!\mathbb {R}^{\text {H}}\) per hidden dimension and a global sampling rate \(\text {T}\_\text {s}\). With this constraint in mind, we investigate each layer \(L\) of our NN as a set of discrete transfer functions with magnitude frequency responses \(\Vert {{{\textbf {G}}}}\_{L,\text {T}\_n}(e^{j2\pi f \text {T}\_n})\Vert \!\in \!\mathbb {R}^{\text {O}\times \text {Y}}\), with \(\text {O}\) outputs, \(\text {Y}\) inputs, and the layer’s actual sampling rate \(\text {T}\_n\). *et al.* Efficient and interpretable raw audio classification with diagonal state space models.

results.content: We compare the frequency response of the discretized system with the frequency response of the original continuous-time system multiplied by the transfer function of the ZoH operator. Ts = 1 # Sample interval Z = (1 - delay(Ts))/(Ts*s) # The transfer function of the ZoH operator Pd = c2d(P, Ts) # Discrete-time system obtained by ZoH sampling Pz = P*Z # The continuous-time version of the discrete-time system wd = exp10.(-2:0.01:log10(2*0.5)) bodeplot(P, wd, lab="\$P(s)\$") bodeplot!(Pz, wd, lab="\$P(s)Z(s)\$") bodeplot!(Pd, wd, lab="\$P_d(z)\$ (ZoH sampling)", l=:dash) vline!([0.5 0.5], l=(:black, :dash), lab="Nyquist freq.", legend=:bottomleft). The step response of `Pz` $= P(s) Z(s)$ matches the discrete output of $P\_d(z)$ delayed by half the sample time. Discrete-time systems can be converted to continuous-time systems formulated with delay terms in such a way that the frequency-response of the two systems match exactly, using the substitution $z^{-1} = e^{-sT\_s}$. This is useful when analyzing hybrid systems with both continuous-time and discrete-time components and accurate frequency-domain calculations are required over the entire frequency range up to the Nyquist frequency. Below, we compare the frequency response of a discrete-time system with delays to two continuous-time systems, one translated using the exact method and one using the standard `d2c` method with inverse ZoH sampling. We see that the translation of the discrete-time system to continuous time using the standard inverse ZoH sampling (`d2c(Pd)`) is not accurate for frequencies close to and above the Nyquist frequency. results.content: Drag image here or click to upload. or paste image `Ctrl` `V` here. * Home / Inverse Laplace Transform Calculator. # Inverse Laplace Transform Calculator. Enter the function into input box and click calculate button to calculate Laplace's inverse by using inverse Laplace transform calculator. * What is meant by inverse Laplace transform? * Examples of Inverse Laplace Transform. ## Inverse Laplace Transform Calculator. Inverse Laplace Transform calculator is used to evaluate the inverse Laplace transform of a given function. This Inverse Laplace calculator will give the result with steps. ## What is meant by inverse Laplace transform? The inverse Laplace transform is the method to transform a given function into the function of time. Inverse Laplace transform is a mathematical technique for taking the inverse of a Laplace transform function. Inverse Laplace transform is also known as inverse Laplace or inverse Laplace transformation. It is denoted as L-1(f(t)). If F(s) is the Laplace transform of the function is f(t). then the inverse transformation is defined as an operator which maps f(t) to F(s). Symbolically it is written as. f(t) = L-1(F(s)), F(s) = L(f(t)). ### **Formula:**. The inverse Laplace transformation in the integral form is given as:. $$L^{-1}\left[F\left(s\right)\right]=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int \_{\left(a-i∞\right)}^{\left(a+i∞\right)}F\left(s\right)\:e^{ts}\:ds$$. ## Examples of Inverse Laplace Transform. We have to discuss some functions to find the Laplace inverse to understand the mathematical way how to calculate it. Find the inverse Laplace transformation of the function 9/(s-3) + 1/(13s+5) +9/(s5). **Step 1:** We have to first convert the given terms in the standard form to apply the formula:. L-1(s) = 9/(s-(-3)) – 1/13(s-5/13) +9 (4!)/4! **Step 2:** Now using the formula 1/s-n = en and 1/sn+1 = tn. L-1(s) **=** 9e-3t- e5/13/13 + 9/24 t4. Find the Laplace inverse transformation of the function s/(s2+7)+1/s2**.**. **Step 1:** Taking the inverses separately we have. L-1(s/(s2+7)) **=** cos(71/2t). L-1 (1/s2) = t. **Step 2:** Now combine the terms together, we have. L-1 (s/(s2+7)+1/s2)=cos(71/2t) + t. ### Math Tools. To calculate result you have to disable your ad blocker first.
